mcqs.question: Which layer of the box model is transparent and never displays the element's own background color?
mcqs.explanation: Margin sits outside the border and is always transparent — it only pushes neighboring boxes away. Padding shares the content's background because it's inside the border, which is why clicking padded space on a button still activates it.

mcqs.question: An element has `width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 2px solid` and `box-sizing: content-box`. How wide does it render?
mcqs.explanation: content-box means width sets only the content area, so padding and border are added on top: 200 + 20 + 20 + 2 + 2 = 244px. Under border-box the same declaration would render at exactly 200px, since padding and border would be carved out of the set width instead.

mcqs.question: Why does `inline-block` exist when both `block` and `inline` are already available?
options: It removes the element from normal flow entirely, like absolute positioning
It disables margin and padding to simplify inline layouts
It lets an element flow next to text like inline, while still respecting width, height, and vertical margin like block
It is a legacy alias for `display: flex` kept for backward compatibility
mcqs.explanation: inline-block combines inline's flow behavior (sits beside other content instead of forcing a line break) with block's sizing behavior (width/height and vertical margin are respected) — plain inline elements ignore width/height entirely. It has nothing to do with removing an element from flow or with flexbox.

mcqs.question: Two stacked paragraphs have `margin-bottom: 20px` and `margin-top: 30px` respectively. How large is the visible gap between them in normal flow?
options: 0px, because inline margins override block margins
mcqs.explanation: Adjacent vertical margins between block-level siblings in normal flow collapse to the larger value rather than summing, so the gap is 30px, not 50px. This only applies to vertical margins in normal flow — it never happens inside flex or grid containers.

mcqs.question: A `div` set to `width: 100%` inside its parent visibly overflows the parent's right edge once you add padding. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The parent element has `overflow: hidden` applied
The child's margin is collapsing with the parent's margin
The child is `display: inline`, so width is being ignored
The child (or a global reset) is missing `box-sizing: border-box`, so the padding is adding to the 100% width instead of being carved out of it
mcqs.explanation: Under the default content-box, width describes only the content area, so any padding adds extra pixels beyond the parent's 100% — the classic cause of an unexpected horizontal overflow. border-box would make the padding eat into the set width instead of adding to it; the other two options don't produce this symptom.
